item.title: Emanuel Navarrete vs O’Shaquie Foster: Live blog, round-by-round and results
item.description: Emanuel Navarrete and O’Shaquie Foster are set to square off in a big title unification at 130 lbs tonight, with three belts on the line, as well as the clear claim to the No. 1 spot in the super featherweight division. Navarrete will be putting his IBF and WBO titles on the line against Foster’s WBC belt in what is definitely the most highly-anticipated fight at 130 lbs this year. Wil Esco will lead the call for us this evening, with updates and results for the three undercard bouts, then live, round-by-round updates for the main event. Join us tonight! Navarrete vs Foster live blog Frank Martin def. Tarik Zaina by TKO in Round 7. Frank Martin was struggling a bit in this appearance, never really getting out of second gear until he found a clean counter left in the seventh that set up the eventual stoppage. Martin, himself, would admit he didn’t performance as he would’ve hoped, but was still content to have scored a stoppage win. THE REFEREE HAS TO INTERVENE WITH MARTIN ON THE ATTACK! MARTIN TKO-7 (2:38). MARTIN DROPS ZAINA HARD IN THE 7TH! Zaina having intermittent success with his long range punching. I have Martin with a one round lead after five. Zaina has a good third round, landing a couple of really good power shots. Martin seemingly has the early edge but not by much. He seems a little tentative and Zaina is fighting a cagey fight. The crowd isn’t particularly pleased through two rounds. D eric “Scooter” Davis def. Joaquin Faccio by Unanimous Decision Official Scores: 80-72, 80-72, 80-72 for Deric “Scooter” Davis. Faccio withstood a tremendous amount of punishment to the body to make it to the final bell. We’re going to the cards but I’ve basically got it a shutout for Scooter. Vicious body attack comes from Scooter in the 6th, Faccio trying to match but can’t quite match the craft. Scooter scoring clean and clear, and more consistently. I’ve got him up 4-0, halfway through the fight. Man, this Faccio character has some awkward footwork that I suppose is meant to be flashy, but it doesn’t seem to actually serve any tactical purpose unless it’s like some weird psychological warfare. Faccio the aggressor but Scooter picking him off with sharp and straight punches, showcasing some good defensive maneuvering in the opening round. How to watch Navarrete vs Foster Start time: 8 pm ET Streaming: DAZN (subscription) Location: Frost Bank Center – San Antonio, TX, USA Navarrete vs Foster main card lineup Emanuel Navarrete vs O’Shaquie Foster , super featherweights, 12 rounds, unification for Navarrete’s IBF and WBO titles and Foster’s WBC title Albert Gonzalez vs Edward Vazquez , featherweights, 10 rounds Frank Martin vs Tarik Zaina , super lightweights, 10 rounds Deric “Scooter” Davis vs Joaquin Faccio , lightweights, 8 rounds Note: Steven Navarro was originally slated to face Emanuel Moreno on the main card, but the fight was canceled after Navarro missed weight.

item.title: Alvarez’s apology goal hands Atlético a sixth consecutive league win
item.description: MADRID, SPAIN - OCTOBER 24: Julian Alvarez of Atletico Madrid scores his team’s first goal as Leo Roman of Real Club Deportivo de A Coruna fails to make a save during the LaLiga EA Sports 2026/27 match between Atletico de Madrid and RC Deportivo de A Coruna at Riyadh Air Metropolitano on October 24, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. (Photo by Angel Martinez/Getty Images) | Getty Images Atlético Madrid have now won six in a row in La Liga, with a Julián Alvarez goal just after halftime enough to see off Deportivo A Coruña at the Metropolitano. The win stretches their unbeaten run to eight games across all competitions, seven wins and a draw, and equals their third-best start to a league season after 10 games. Diego Simeone was clear earlier this week that Atleti can challenge Barcelona, and this win moves the Rojiblancos to within two points of the league leaders. Tomorrow’s Clásico result could go a long way toward defining this early-season narrative. For now, let’s dive into the takeaways from today. Slow out the blocks, again After a very poor first half in Stuttgart earlier in the week, Atleti carried right on in that vein at home. The hosts never really wanted to seize the initiative – seven shots, none of which troubled Leo Román in goal. In truth, it was Deportivo who should have led, when Lorenzo Amatucci should have tapped in from close range after a dangerous Yeremay Hernández free kick. For the most part, it felt like Atleti were missing Jonathan David. He has stepped up so unexpectedly to become such a crucial part of this side that his absence is now felt in a big way. Nearly every attack lacked a presence in the box, and it looked a lot like the early-season games, before the window shut and David arrived. Only Lee Kang-in managed a shot from inside the penalty area in the first half, which says plenty about the quality of chances Atleti were creating. In seasons past, this is exactly the sort of game Deportivo would have scored in and turned the evening on its head. Credit where it is due to the defense, though. Jan Oblak was brilliant yet again, and the back line in front of him, despite a few lapses in concentration, recovered and held on for the most part. The improvement in that department, even with Cristian Romero’s injury problems, cannot be understated. It gives Atleti a platform to stay in games, especially when they start as slowly as they did here. He was dropping too deep, giving his teammates nothing to aim for inside the box, and it really hampered Atleti’s chance creation. There were whistles. item.content:encoded: MADRID, SPAIN - OCTOBER 24: Julian Alvarez of Atletico Madrid scores his team’s first goal as Leo Roman of Real Club Deportivo de A Coruna fails to make a save during the LaLiga EA Sports 2026/27 match between Atletico de Madrid and RC Deportivo de A Coruna at Riyadh Air Metropolitano on October 24, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. (Photo by Angel Martinez/Getty Images) | Getty Images Atlético Madrid have now won six in a row in La Liga, with a Julián Alvarez goal just after halftime enough to see off Deportivo A Coruña at the Metropolitano. The win stretches their unbeaten run to eight games across all competitions, seven wins and a draw, and equals their third-best start to a league season after 10 games. Diego Simeone was clear earlier this week that Atleti can challenge Barcelona, and this win moves the Rojiblancos to within two points of the league leaders. Tomorrow’s Clásico result could go a long way toward defining this early-season narrative. For now, let’s dive into the takeaways from today. Slow out the blocks, again After a very poor first half in Stuttgart earlier in the week, Atleti carried right on in that vein at home. The hosts never really wanted to seize the initiative – seven shots, none of which troubled Leo Román in goal. In truth, it was Deportivo who should have led, when Lorenzo Amatucci should have tapped in from close range after a dangerous Yeremay Hernández free kick. For the most part, it felt like Atleti were missing Jonathan David. He has stepped up so unexpectedly to become such a crucial part of this side that his absence is now felt in a big way. Nearly every attack lacked a presence in the box, and it looked a lot like the early-season games, before the window shut and David arrived. Only Lee Kang-in managed a shot from inside the penalty area in the first half, which says plenty about the quality of chances Atleti were creating. In seasons past, this is exactly the sort of game Deportivo would have scored in and turned the evening on its head. Credit where it is due to the defense, though. Jan Oblak was brilliant yet again, and the back line in front of him, despite a few lapses in concentration, recovered and held on for the most part. The improvement in that department, even with Cristian Romero’s injury problems, cannot be understated. It gives Atleti a platform to stay in games, especially when they start as slowly as they did here. Apologies on and off the pitch In that first half, it looked like another questionable Julián performance. He was dropping too deep, giving his teammates nothing to aim for inside the box, and it really hampered Atleti’s chance creation. There were whistles. Not as many as when he first returned to the side, but they were still there. For much of those 45 minutes, I thought this might be one of those games where he is brought off to give the other in-form attackers a chance of finding three points. Then came the moment . It had been 347 days since Alvarez last scored in La Liga at the Metropolitano, and 395 since his last league goal from open play. Early in the second half, he finally crashed the box. There was a clear shift in Atleti’s approach, with more players committed forward and driving into the area, and Alvarez’s goal arrived when Alejandro Grimaldo slipped him an inch-perfect ball to tap home. A goal in midweek in Stuttgart, an assist at Espanyol last weekend, and now, finally, a goal at the Metropolitano. The week of La Araña’s apology on the pitch. View this post on Instagram If the reaction of the majority, though not all, of the crowd is anything to go by, the more Alvarez keeps scoring, the easier it will be for them to forget past misgivings and accept him back. The Spidey celebration did come out, but notably not toward the supporters as it usually is. It was a more muted version, aimed at the sidelines. There is still some way to go before he can turn and face them . And then, as I was putting together my thoughts on the on-pitch apology, an off-pitch one followed. In his post-match interview, Alvarez apologized directly to the fans. He said the supporters have “always been very generous” with him, and that what he said during the World Cup about wanting a transfer was a mistake on his part, because “it was neither the right moment nor the right way to handle things.” He added that he understood the anger and would have been angry too if he were a fan, that he now has to focus on improving, and that “it is time to compete for everything.” Truth be told, there will not be a better time for Alvarez to start winning the fans back. Atlético head into a key stretch of the season with some massive games to come. Bayern Munich visit the Metropolitano in the Champions League at the start of November, and five days later, Barcelona arrive in the league. That second game would be the first time Alvarez faces the Blaugrana since pushing all summer for a move to join them. We may still not have the Alvarez of the last couple of seasons back, but today marks another major turning point in this saga. A goal against the league leaders in two weeks would go a long way toward mending the relationship between player and supporters. Early Halloween scare Atleti should have come away from this game a bit more comfortably, but they squandered a few really good chances. Pretty tellingly though, they actually conceded the better ones. The xG finished at 1.37 for the Rojiblancos and 1.95 for Deportivo. The image of Kevin Sánchez’s miss in the dying seconds is already circulating on social media . Adama Traoré whipped in an excellent cross that found the Spaniard inside the six-yard box, and the chance looked harder to miss than to score. Eventually though, Oblak gratefully collected the ball in his arms after looking well beaten. Between that and Amatucci’s chance in the first half, the hosts really pushed the limits, toeing the line between a win and dropped points. The end result is still positive, and the general feeling after this one should be too. The good news is that this side can win without being at its best, something Atleti missed in past seasons, the consistency of picking up points on days like this. But there are warning signs showing despite the run of form. If Atleti want to show they are capable of winning silverware this year, they will need to see out games better and capitalize when they are ahead. Between Alvarez’s goal in the 48th minute and Deportivo’s late flurry, Atleti outshot their opponents 11-2, and on a number of attacks they looked favorites to get the second goal that would have sealed the points. Alexander Sørloth’s introduction brought more energy, and watching back some of those sequences, it almost seems harder to explain how Simeone’s side did not find a second. That is now four of the six wins in this run that the Rojiblancos have taken by a single goal. Real Madrid is one thing, but Alavés, Espanyol and Deportivo A Coruña are exactly the kind of opponents you would expect them to beat more comfortably than they have. It is very positive that Atleti keep finding ways to pull wins out of the bag. But dropping points in games like these can prove costly over the course of a season, and this was another warning sign that things may not always be as green as they seem. Heed it, start seeing games out better, and close the door properly once the breakthrough comes. Halloween is around the corner, but no more last-second scares, please.

item.title: Bloomington South volleyball wins first regional since 1977
item.description: BLOOMINGTON — Bloomington South's volleyball team acted like it had been there before. The Panthers stubbed their toe in last year's regional match against Castle . One year later, they brought back most of the same players, but were a much different team. Lessons absorbed, South was confident and on point with a nearly perfect start that launched a 25-11, 25-14, 25-17 sweep of young, outmanned Columbus East in the Class 4A Bloomington North Regional on Saturday, Oct. 24. For the first time since 1977, South is a regional champ. More: Bloomington South, North, Edgewood cross country all send reps to state More: Bloomington South doubles team takes second at state championships "Whenever I heard that stat, that drove me," South senior middle Quinn Reynolds said. "I really wanted to win after hearing we hadn't won since the 70s. And I knew this was the team that we can go far with, so that's really exciting to have ended that (streak)." “That's crazy," senior libero Neely Warner said. "I'm so proud of our team." Edgewood (2011-12) was the last county program to win a regional with North last making the elite eight in 2005 when the IHSAA had four-team regionals. And with a 29-2 record, this team is now the school record holder for most wins in a season and moves on to semi-state, where the Panthers will face another rematch with Center Grove (32-4), a four-set winner over Brownsburg. The other pairing has Floyd Central (29-5) taking on Yorktown (29-2). Those matches will take place at Jennings County Saturday, Oct. 31, with the early semifinal winners advancing to the championship match at night. Match times were not announced as of late Saturday night. "It's amazing," South coach Emma Abplanalp said. "This group, they want it bad and they wanted this game. We were just here a year ago and I said we'd be back if we'd figure it out, and they did. They spent the whole offseason, in-season all 31 games for this moment." Made for the moment Getting over the regional hump meant meeting the moment when it came, no matter the opponent or the final result. Seven seniors have led the way. "That entailed winning all the games we should and trying our hardest and playing our best when we shouldn't," Abplanalp said. "We still have those two losses, but in the postseason, those don't matter. "Just one game at a time and knowing that we can face adversity and challenges and those lulls in games and that we can find a way." Columbus East (14-17), a young team with just one senior, was a bit of a surprise opponent but one they knew well. And South knew how to deal with an underdog, taking away their hopes of an upset from the start and killing the Olympians with demoralizing long runs and strong finishes to each set. "Whatever speed is on the other side of the court, we play our speed," Abplanalp said. "And I think that really showed first set." Strong serving had the Olympians out of system early and often and plenty of free balls for South's offense to feast on.

One year later, they brought back most of the same players, but were a much different team. Lessons absorbed, South was confident and on point with a nearly perfect start that launched a 25-11, 25-14, 25-17 sweep of young, outmanned Columbus East in the Class 4A Bloomington North Regional on Saturday, Oct. 24. For the first time since 1977, South is a regional champ. More: Bloomington South, North, Edgewood cross country all send reps to state More: Bloomington South doubles team takes second at state championships "Whenever I heard that stat, that drove me," South senior middle Quinn Reynolds said. "I really wanted to win after hearing we hadn't won since the 70s. And I knew this was the team that we can go far with, so that's really exciting to have ended that (streak)." “That's crazy," senior libero Neely Warner said. "I'm so proud of our team." Edgewood (2011-12) was the last county program to win a regional with North last making the elite eight in 2005 when the IHSAA had four-team regionals. Those matches will take place at Jennings County Saturday, Oct. 31, with the early semifinal winners advancing to the championship match at night. Match times were not announced as of late Saturday night. "It's amazing," South coach Emma Abplanalp said. "This group, they want it bad and they wanted this game. We were just here a year ago and I said we'd be back if we'd figure it out, and they did. They spent the whole offseason, in-season all 31 games for this moment." Made for the moment Getting over the regional hump meant meeting the moment when it came, no matter the opponent or the final result. Seven seniors have led the way. "That entailed winning all the games we should and trying our hardest and playing our best when we shouldn't," Abplanalp said. "We still have those two losses, but in the postseason, those don't matter. "Just one game at a time and knowing that we can face adversity and challenges and those lulls in games and that we can find a way." Columbus East (14-17), a young team with just one senior, was a bit of a surprise opponent but one they knew well. And South knew how to deal with an underdog, taking away their hopes of an upset from the start and killing the Olympians with demoralizing long runs and strong finishes to each set. "Whatever speed is on the other side of the court, we play our speed," Abplanalp said. "And I think that really showed first set." Strong serving had the Olympians out of system early and often and plenty of free balls for South's offense to feast on. Set 1, South led 7-5 before going up 16-7 and burying Columbus East the rest of the way. The Panthers finished with no attack errors and no service errors with 14 kills, three aces and two blocks. "We just really know how to set the tone, and we wanted to make sure we took care of business fast and early," senior setter Harper Rahn said. Set 2, it was 5-5 when South scored the next nine points, went side-outs to lead 20-13 and scored five of the last six points. Set 3 was a bit closer, but South turned a 15-11 lead into a 20-11 advantage after an Everly Clark ace. "It's fun to have momentum," Neely said. "When we're all having fun, it just shows." South looked comfortable, and it showed. "I think some of last year helped," Abplanalp said. "We got to play in this game and the first thing, we walk in, it's loud, there's a lot of people here. We weren't ready for that last year. We hadn't played in those conditions a lot. "This year, we knew what to expect. But also this group, most of this roster played last season. We have experience. Not a lot rattles this team. But I also can't downplay how much hard work they've put in this season. They have worked their butts off and I think that's really showing here in this postseason." There was just one small hiccup, coming after South took a 20-11 lead in the third. The Panthers could see the finish line and made four errors to let the Olympians score five in a row and force Abplanalp to use her first and only timeout of the night. "That was definitely a little nervous," Reynolds said. "But I knew that we were going to be able to lock in." In fact, Reynolds was the only who put the next swing away and the Panthers were back on track to celebrating a huge breakthrough with friends and family. "Not much talking in the huddle. It was a pretty quick huddle," Abplanalp said. "Just reminding them, who you have as hitters and what's open and how to get out of that. "They were still calm. We're good." This article originally appeared on The Herald-Times: Bloomington South volleyball wins first regional since 1977

Sherwood intercepted a pass and took it to the net. 8:26 p.m.: Right as the Sharks' penalty is up, Dmitry Orlov will replace Marchment in the box for tripping. 8:23 p.m.: Mason Marchment gets 2 minutes for interference on Hampus Lindholm. It'll be 4-on-4 for about 40 seconds. Bruins came close to scoring while a man short. Bruins are full strength and have the man advantage for 2 minutes. 8:21 p.m.: Nikita Zadorov gets a minor for slashing. Sharks will have the advantage for the third time tonight. Zadorov has 15 penalty minutes over the last 5 games. Bruins 2, Sharks 1 8:19 p.m.: Marat Khusnutdinov slips one by Nedeljkovic to give the Bruins the lead. They used the whole offensive depth, and it worked out. Geekie and Minten were credited with the assist. 92 knocks its home. https://t.co/9xEA5ZYnlx — Boston Bruins (@NHLBruins) October 25, 2026 8:16 p.m.: Just heard from the playcallers that the Bruins were not credited with a shot on goal during their first power play. Boston is getting messy. Zacha was wide-open and sent the shot too high and too wide to the right. Would have been a perfect goal. 8:14 p.m.: Bruins are struggling to convert in the neutral zone. Sharks are full strength. 8:09 p.m.: Bruins get their first power play of the night. Ty Dellandrea gets a minor for tripping. 8:05 p.m.: Elias Lindholm wins the face-off against Celebrini to start the second period. End of first period: Bruins 1, Sharks 1 7:44 p.m.: Sharks are leading in time of possession. Swayman came out of the net to slow the puck and almost didn't make it back in when the Sharks got a hold of the puck. Some defenders helped cover while Swayman got back into place. 7:42 p.m.: Pavel Zacha had a nice attempted tip-in. 7:40 p.m.: Collin Graf subtly tries to tip the puck in, but Swayman is on top of it and stops the puck. 7:36 p.m.: Bruins survive this penalty kill. item.title: There will be even less drag in Cup cars at Talladega on Sunday
item.description: Motorsport photo Ultimately, one half an inch fewer of spoiler is not expected to fundamentally change the racing at Talladega on Sunday but everyone in the Cup Series field is expecting continued directional positivity. For the summer race at Daytona, NASCAR reduced the rear spoiler length from 7” to 4” to reduce the overall drag on the NextGen during superspeedway races. Drivers generally felt they could better jump out of line and make more efficient runs with the changes so NASCAR is taking it a step further this weekend with a 3.5” spoiler. Denny Hamlin likes the general direction officials have taken this package. “I still think that this was a positive direction and I absolutely felt that there was more space between the cars at Daytona than what we've had in years past,” Hamlin said on Saturday at Talladega. “So, I think that this is another little, small step compared to the big step we took there, but again, it's incrementally in the right direction. “But this racetrack races differently. It's a little bit wider. So, the runs aren't quite as big here as they are at Daytona. There are a lot of outside factors that we really are not going to know until it all plays out. “But certainly, a day race here is also going to make it a little bit slicker as well. Again, I’m going to find out exactly when you do.” Hamlin articulates it that way because NASCAR does not currently allow for superspeedway practice sessions. In other words, as was the case at Daytona in the summer, no one will know what has changed until they start racing it. Read Also: NASCAR Cup title contenders living on a prayer at Talladega NASCAR plans to modify Phoenix dogleg to lessen driver loads Joey Logano enjoyed that process at Daytona and is expecting the same on Sunday. “Yeah, I feel the same way because there’s still a lot of unknowns.” Ditto Chase Elliott . “I kind of enjoyed the unknown at Daytona,” Elliott said. :I thought it was kind of fun, just having absolutely no idea what to expect. I think there’ll be another element of that here this weekend. I do think that just the conditions and the track surface can play a big role in that too.” In other words, Elliott is saying some of what happens on Sunday will just be the difference in temperatures and intensity from the early May race to the late October race. It will be much cooler weekend than the previous race. It’s a similar dynamic in how the Daytona 500 and Firecracker 400 differ from each other. “You know, I will say that throughout the course of my career, I feel like I have always complained about balance the least at the Daytona night race,” Elliott said. “And I just think in general, the level of aggression that you can have in that race with the temperature, typically the sun being off the racetrack and the surface being somewhat new — I shouldn’t say new, but has a fair amount of grip to it, it has always kind of surprised me how different the Daytona 500 feels to that race.” William Byron said there was

In other words, there was more grip and stability than they anticipated. “Some guys went the conservative route with their trim levels,” Byron said. “I feel like, this weekend, some guys will trim out even more having some confidence in what this package will do. “I think you will see potentially faster speeds this and there’s less spoiler this weekend too. This car has been a head scratcher sometimes. item.title: Jaguars WR/CB Travis Hunter fined nearly $15K by NFL for removing helmet
item.description: A Jacksonville Jaguars player was hit with another fine by the NFL this week, which has been sort of rubbing it in since Jags fans are convinced the officials are especially flag-happy when it comes to working a game with a team in teal and black. And the latest was the biggest fine yet, and for a guy who was just happy in the moment. Cornerback/wide receiver Travis Hunter was fined $14,926 for removing his helmet when he celebrated his first career interception against the Houston Texans on Oct. 18 during the Jags' 34-31 loss at London's Wembley Stadium. Hunter's interception came in the end zone to halt a Houston drive, just after he scored a touchdown on a pass from Trevor Lawrence to get the Jaguars ' within three points. Ryan O'Halloran: Do the Jaguars have a penalty problem? Lawrence guided the offense into position for a 60-yard field goal by Cam Little so Hunter's two big plays were a potential swing of 17 points. The Jags lost on Ka'imi Fairbairn's 49-yard field goal on the game's last play. Hunter is the eighth Jaguars player to be fined by the NFL and the first to get fined even though a penalty was not called during the game. The fines total nearly $80,000. Jaguars players fined by NFL this season Travis Hunter, $14,926 vs. Houston, removal of helmet Bryan Thomas Jr., $4,972 vs. Philadelphia, fight on first play Jarrian Jones, $8,201 vs. Cincinnati, face mask penalty Travon Walker, $11,941 vs. Cincinnati, taunting Arik Armstead, $11,941 vs. New England, unnecessary roughness Nate Boerkircher, $8,025 vs. New England, chop block Robert Hainsey, $6,750 vs. New England, unnecessary roughness, low block Antonio Johnson, $12,537 vs. New England, unnecessary roughness, striking/kicking/kneeing What happens to the fine money? Fines are deducted from the players' next game check, unless he appeals and wins. According to the NFL, fines are donated to the Professional Athletes Foundation "to support Legends in need" and the NFL Foundation "to further support the health, safety and wellness of athletes across all levels, including youth football and the communities that support the game." The NFL said that nearly $4 million per year in fines has gone to those organizations since 2011. This article originally appeared on Florida Times-Union: Jaguars WR/CB Travis Hunter fined nearly $15K by NFL for removing helmet

item.title: Peyton Bowen keeps making 'game-changing plays' as OU football beats MSU | Report card
item.description: STARKVILLE, MS — Oklahoma ’s offense had a banner day. Better than the scoreboard showed in OU’s 23-15 win against Mississippi State on Saturday in Starkville. The Sooners’ 467 yards were its most-ever against a conference opponent since joining the SEC. Let’s get to the grades. More: John Mateer nearly flawless in leading OU football past Mississippi State | 5 takeaways Peyton Bowen: A+ If you want to see Brent Venables light up, just ask him about Peyton Bowen. The senior safety had another huge game, snagging a timely pick in the end zone midway through the fourth quarter. . “He’s made a ton of game-changing plays,” Venables said. Bowen and the Sooners defense limited the Bulldogs to a 1-of-11 conversion rate on third down. OU’s four sacks and six tackles for a loss were its most in both categories in conference play. Mississippi State star quarterback Kamario Taylor tried to give it a go, but he clearly wasn’t right. Backup Jimmy Puckett fared OK in a difficult spot. Tate Sandell: D Tate Sandell is no longer a sure thing. Far from it. Last year’s Lou Groza Award winner went 3 for 6 Saturday, with makes of 30, 38 and 42 yards and misses from 41, 45 and 45 yards. (On the 41-yard miss, Sandell had been good from 36 yards, but he had to rekick — unsuccessfully — after the Sooners were penalized for illegal formation). Sandell went 23 for 24 on field goals last regular season before missing two kicks against Alabama in the first round of the College Football Playoff. Sandell has struggled since, but he’s in no danger of losing his job. Big plays: A OU’s longest pass of the season and longest run of the season came in the same quarter Saturday in Starkville. Tory Blaylock got the third quarter started with a 47-yard run. Later in the quarter, John Mateer connected with Isaiah Sategna III on a 54-yard pass. Mateer had five passes of 20-plus yards, tying his season high. Rocky Beers: C- OU tight end Rocky Beers caught a 32-yard touchdown to give the Sooners a 17-0 lead early in the third quarter. Then Beers gave it right back. On OU’s next drive, Beers fumbled while hurdling a Mississippi State defender. If there was one thing OU couldn’t afford to do, it was that. The Bulldogs were given new life, and they made good on it — scoring on a double pass to draw within 10. Beers had an even worse blunder later in the third quarter, dropping an easy touchdown catch that would’ve given the Sooners a 24-7 lead. Killer penalties: C- OU had three of them in the first half. At the end of the first quarter, a Peyton Joseph chop block erased a would-be first down. The Sooners should’ve been in automatic scoring territory, but they came away with nothing after Tate Sandell missed a 45-yard field goal attempt. In the second quarter, OU defensive end Taylor Wein jumped offsides on a fourth-and-2 that Mississippi State — deep in its own territory — surely wasn’t going for. The Bulldogs were just trying to get the Sooners to jump. Wein made another senseless play late
item.content:encoded: STARKVILLE, MS — Oklahoma ’s offense had a banner day. Better than the scoreboard showed in OU’s 23-15 win against Mississippi State on Saturday in Starkville. The Sooners’ 467 yards were its most-ever against a conference opponent since joining the SEC. Let’s get to the grades. More: John Mateer nearly flawless in leading OU football past Mississippi State | 5 takeaways Peyton Bowen: A+ If you want to see Brent Venables light up, just ask him about Peyton Bowen. The senior safety had another huge game, snagging a timely pick in the end zone midway through the fourth quarter. . “He’s made a ton of game-changing plays,” Venables said. Bowen and the Sooners defense limited the Bulldogs to a 1-of-11 conversion rate on third down. OU’s four sacks and six tackles for a loss were its most in both categories in conference play. Mississippi State star quarterback Kamario Taylor tried to give it a go, but he clearly wasn’t right. Backup Jimmy Puckett fared OK in a difficult spot. Tate Sandell: D Tate Sandell is no longer a sure thing. Far from it. Last year’s Lou Groza Award winner went 3 for 6 Saturday, with makes of 30, 38 and 42 yards and misses from 41, 45 and 45 yards. (On the 41-yard miss, Sandell had been good from 36 yards, but he had to rekick — unsuccessfully — after the Sooners were penalized for illegal formation). Sandell went 23 for 24 on field goals last regular season before missing two kicks against Alabama in the first round of the College Football Playoff. Sandell has struggled since, but he’s in no danger of losing his job. Big plays: A OU’s longest pass of the season and longest run of the season came in the same quarter Saturday in Starkville. Tory Blaylock got the third quarter started with a 47-yard run. Later in the quarter, John Mateer connected with Isaiah Sategna III on a 54-yard pass. Mateer had five passes of 20-plus yards, tying his season high. Rocky Beers: C- OU tight end Rocky Beers caught a 32-yard touchdown to give the Sooners a 17-0 lead early in the third quarter. Then Beers gave it right back. On OU’s next drive, Beers fumbled while hurdling a Mississippi State defender. If there was one thing OU couldn’t afford to do, it was that. The Bulldogs were given new life, and they made good on it — scoring on a double pass to draw within 10. Beers had an even worse blunder later in the third quarter, dropping an easy touchdown catch that would’ve given the Sooners a 24-7 lead. Killer penalties: C- OU had three of them in the first half. At the end of the first quarter, a Peyton Joseph chop block erased a would-be first down. The Sooners should’ve been in automatic scoring territory, but they came away with nothing after Tate Sandell missed a 45-yard field goal attempt. In the second quarter, OU defensive end Taylor Wein jumped offsides on a fourth-and-2 that Mississippi State — deep in its own territory — surely wasn’t going for. The Bulldogs were just trying to get the Sooners to jump. Wein made another senseless play later in the second quarter, getting whistled for a personal foul at the end of a punt. Mississippi State returned the favor, giving OU a critical first down on the Sooners’ scoring drive at the end of the first half. A fourth-quarter illegal formation penalty wiped away three OU points. The teams kept trading ill-timed penalties. After Sandell’s miss, Mississippi State put together a nice drive and got all the way to the 1-yard line on a 27-yard pass to Zion Ragins. The play, though, was wiped away due to holding. Mississippi State got backed up, and Peyton Bowen promptly picked off Jimmy Puckett. Ball game. More: Who is Sean Hutton? OU football team honors injured OL with helmet stickers Mississippi State Sooners: A+ Mississippi State’s pregame hype video was voiced by none other than former Longhorn turned Sooner turned Mississippi State Bulldog Brenen Thompson, who’s now playing for the Chargers. And on the first play from scrimmage, Mississippi State quarterback Kamario Taylor tried to connect with former Sooner Zion Ragins on a deep shot. You think Jeff Lebby dialed that one up for a reason? Former Sooner Kendel Dolby recovered Rocky Beers’ fumble in the third quarter. The chef’s kiss came at the end of the first quarter, when the Mississippi State softball team was honored on the field. The team, coached by former Sooner Samantha Ricketts, that stunned OU in the super regionals last spring. You have to respect it. Starkville experience: A- Starkville gets a bad rap. Its name does it no favors. But here’s my theory: Most who knock Starkville and Mississippi State have never been there. Sure, it’s an outpost — especially for those who prefer to fly (I very much recommend driving from Oklahoma). And yes, it’s very small. About half the size (25,000 people) of Stillwater. But I found Starkville to be a perfectly fine place. It was my second time here, but I didn’t remember much from nine years ago (covering Kentucky-Mississippi State) outside of the football stadium. Granted, most of what I saw in Starkville was in the dark, and I don’t pretend that you can get a feel for a town being there for less than 48 hours. Our crew, which included me, OU beat writer Colton Sulley and old friends Berry Tramel and Mason Young of the Tulsa World, pulled into Starkville a little after 7 p.m. Friday. We had dinner at Lost Pizza Co., a southeast-based chain with a couple of locations in Texas. Thumbs up all around. Then it was off to Bop’s Frozen Custard for a sweet treat. It’s an old-school stand with a walk-up window and two drive-thru lanes. It reminded me of Ted Drewes in St. Louis. I found Mississippi State’s campus and game-day atmosphere to be on par with much of what you see in the SEC. Tons of tailgating tents. Plenty of character. And the cowbell clanging is a one-of-one experience. The size of the crowd was the only disappointment. Davis Wade Stadium is the second-smallest stadium in the SEC (61,337) ahead of only Vanderbilt, and it wasn’t close to full. Fans were late arriving and early to leave. The cowbell is the great equalizer, though. This has to be the loudest stadium in college football per capita. Joe Mussatto is a sports columnist for The Oklahoman. Have a story idea for Joe? Email him at jmussatto@oklahoman.com . Support Joe's work and that of other Oklahoman journalists by purchasing a digital subscription today at subscribe.oklahoman.com . item.title: How Valkyries ‘kept punching’ to win WNBA Finals Game 4 vs. Dream
item.description: How Valkyries ‘kept punching’ to win WNBA Finals Game 4 vs. Dream appeared first on ClutchPoints . Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . ATLANTA– Of all the adjustments the Golden State Valkyries had to make heading into Game 4 of the WNBA Finals , down 2-1 in a hostile road environment, none were going to matter unless they rekindled their fire. Reconfiguring their spacing, cutting down on turnovers, guarding Angel Reese: none of it was going to translate unless they got back to playing their brand of basketball. The kind of basketball that suffocates opponents with their endless supply of energy. The kind of basketball that demoralizes teams with their inability to quit. The Valkyries’ way of unselfish, egoless basketball that continues to defy logic, as Veronica Burton said on the eve of Game 4 in the wake of their lowest moment of the season. “There’s been moments in games this season where it feels like there’s no way we’re gonna win this,” Veronica Burton said Friday, on the eve of Game 4. “And you could say that there’s no way the Valkyries are gonna be here, whatever it may be. And you find a way, and you will it out, and you do it together, and you grind it out. That’s what has allowed us to get here… Logistically, it doesn’t make much sense, but you come together, and you find a way to do it, and that’s what it comes down to.” Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) And that’s what it came down to, as Golden State gutted out a 67-62 victory over the Atlanta Dream. Sure, there were tactical adjustments like Natalie Nakase swapping in Tiffany Hayes and Kaila Charles for Cecilia Zandalasini and Kayla Thornton to shake up the starting lineup. And there were schematic changes the Valkyries made, like leaning more on the pick-and-roll and forcing Reese to her left hand. But at the center of the hurricane that was the Valkyries diving on the floor, flying in for rebounds, sprinting back to save layups, had little to do with the X’s and O’s drawn up on the whiteboard. It was the grit they built back in their thunderous 16-point comeback in Game 3 against Dallas Wings. It was the composure they gained from felling five-time MVP A’ja Wilson and the Las Vegas Aces three games in a row in the semifinals. And it was the heart they’ve forged as a collective; as a team unshaken “We had the energy,” an out-of-breath Charles said after the game. “We punched first, and we kind of dictated (the game). And the most important part is obviously they’re a great team, so when they were trying to make their run, we didn’t fold. We didn’t put our heads down. We just continued to keep punching and keep punching, and we were able to get the win.” Brett Davis-Imagn Images The Valkyries must set the tone The Valkyries’ punch began with their star Gabby Williams, who took it upon herself right after Game 3 to fire up the team by giving an animated speech in the post-game huddle. “If I want to lead my team, I have to be the one that sets the ton

The Valkyries’ way of unselfish, egoless basketball that continues to defy logic, as Veronica Burton said on the eve of Game 4 in the wake of their lowest moment of the season. “There’s been moments in games this season where it feels like there’s no way we’re gonna win this,” Veronica Burton said Friday, on the eve of Game 4. “And you could say that there’s no way the Valkyries are gonna be here, whatever it may be. And you find a way, and you will it out, and you do it together, and you grind it out. That’s what has allowed us to get here… Logistically, it doesn’t make much sense, but you come together, and you find a way to do it, and that’s what it comes down to.” Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) And that’s what it came down to, as Golden State gutted out a 67-62 victory over the Atlanta Dream. Sure, there were tactical adjustments like Natalie Nakase swapping in Tiffany Hayes and Kaila Charles for Cecilia Zandalasini and Kayla Thornton to shake up the starting lineup. And there were schematic changes the Valkyries made, like leaning more on the pick-and-roll and forcing Reese to her left hand. But at the center of the hurricane that was the Valkyries diving on the floor, flying in for rebounds, sprinting back to save layups, had little to do with the X’s and O’s drawn up on the whiteboard. It was the grit they built back in their thunderous 16-point comeback in Game 3 against Dallas Wings. It was the composure they gained from felling five-time MVP A’ja Wilson and the Las Vegas Aces three games in a row in the semifinals. And it was the heart they’ve forged as a collective; as a team unshaken “We had the energy,” an out-of-breath Charles said after the game. “We punched first, and we kind of dictated (the game). And the most important part is obviously they’re a great team, so when they were trying to make their run, we didn’t fold. We didn’t put our heads down. We just continued to keep punching and keep punching, and we were able to get the win.” Brett Davis-Imagn Images The Valkyries must set the tone The Valkyries’ punch began with their star Gabby Williams, who took it upon herself right after Game 3 to fire up the team by giving an animated speech in the post-game huddle. “If I want to lead my team, I have to be the one that sets the tone. I have to lead by example,” Williams said of her leadership style and how it changed between Games 3 and 4 after collecting a team-high 17 points. “That motivated me to set the tempo today, start off the game with a lot of aggressiveness. And before the game, I just talked to the team about not having regrets. And that the beauty of our sport is– as bad as we felt on Wednesday, we get to turn around and make it right up today.” That emphasis on starting the game aggressively showed early as the Valkyries wrestled control of the possession battle through sheer will. Whether it was center Kiah Stokes collecting a series-high 16 rebounds, eight of which came on the offensive glass, Williams and Zandalasini lurking in the passing lanes, Charles and Thornton crashing the boards with reckless abandon, or Veronica Burton doing Veronica Burton things, Golden State neutralized their inefficient shooting through brute force. At halftime, Golden State outshot the Dream 40-to-19, won the turnover battle 4-to-13, and dominated the stock differential 8-to-3. But the Dream refused to die, rattling off a 14-4 run in the third quarter that dwindled the Valkyries’ lead to 46-40. But even with the offense stuck in the mud, Golden State began nailing timely buckets, starting with Hayes wrapping a layup around Reese’s outstretched arms to blunt the raucous Atlanta crowd. Still, as crunch time neared and the Dream continued to close the distance, it was clear someone on the Valkyries was going to have to make some big-time shots. And, true to the Valkyries’ ethos, their emphasis on the small, intangible things that add up to winning, Burton, the player who embodies it best, stepped into the spotlight. It was Burton, who’d been smacked in the face and thrown to the floor all game long, who drained a 3-pointer from the wing to put the Valkyries up 64-55 with 4:23 left in the game. It was Burton who spun her way from the contest of Rhyne Howard to nail the decisive dagger to extend the Golden State lead to seven with 33.6 seconds on the clock. It didn’t matter that it wasn’t her night offensively, shooting just 4-of-17 from the field. Because just like she did against the Wings and the Aces, she found her shot when it mattered. “She’s our heart and soul of the team,” Nakase said of Burton’s fight. “Probably like 10 times, she probably got knocked down. That girl is resilient. She’s literally our leader in terms of– never quit, fall down, get back up, things are not going our way, it’s all right. She finished with that shot. She said, ‘ I got it. I got the isolation.’ And she just attacked her matchup and closed it and really calmed us down.” Brett Davis-Imagn Images The Valkyries have tied things up heading into Game 4 But for all the heroics the Valkyries pulled off to tie the series at 2-2, the page turns quickly to Game 5 back home in San Francisco on Monday. “We feel good getting the win. Definitely feel good going home, but we know the job’s not done,” Hayes said. “So in order to finish it out, we gotta continue to play like we did today for most of the time. We had a few lapses, but continue to play like that. We’ll finish it out.” Is it possible for the Valkyries to continue to play like that again? They won the possession battle; they held Reese to just eight points on 2-of-12 shooting; they overcame a 31-13 free-throw differential. Everything went their way, and they won by five. But as Burton said when their backs were against the wall: logic has never applied to the Valkyries. When they have a will, they have a way. And with these finals now essentially a best-of-three series, Golden State has willed their way into a fighting chance. With the 2026 season approaching its conclusion, every position matters. And after a dramatic Progress Group 250 that saw Sammy Smith edge Carson Kvapil by just 0.084 seconds, the championship picture remains competitive at the top. Jesse Love entered Saturday’s race with the points lead and did exactly what he needed to do to protect it. item.title: Trevor Goosby injury update: Texas football LT, projected 1st round pick, leaves game
item.description: Texas offensive lineman Trevor Goosby (74) blocks during the game against Florida at Darrell K Royal–Texas Memorial Stadium on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026 in Austin. (Aaron E. Martinez/Austin American-Statesman) Texas football lost the anchor of its offensive line to injury in the first quarter of Saturday's game against Ole Miss . Longhorns left tackle Trevor Goosby was carted off the field after his leg appeared to buckle while blocking a Rebels defender. Goosby laid on the ground for more than a minute after falling to the turf, and both teams went into their respective huddles at Royal-Memorial Stadium before Goosby was taken to the sideline. Goosby, 21, is a senior and 2025 All-SEC selection. He did not return to the field for the remainder of the first quarter. This story will be updated. item.title: 3 takeaways after the Sooners beat the Bulldogs
item.description: The Oklahoma Sooners defeated the Mississippi State Bulldogs in Starkville on Saturday, winning 23-15 despite a sloppy performance. OU is now 4-3 overall and 2-2 in SEC play, and Brent Venables got the win over former assistant Jeff Lebby. OU was aided by MSU star quarterback Kamario Taylor missing the game's final three quarters, but the defense played well against both Taylor and backup Parker Puckett. Short of a double pass trick play touchdown and a late desperation TD and two-point conversion, the Sooners again put a lot of good on film on the defensive side of the ball. As expected, most of the mistakes came on the offensive side of the ball, but the OU special teams also had a poor day, especially kicker Tate Sandell. Oklahoma got a road win in the SEC, and those are hard to come by, but it's a game that the Sooners should have won by much more. Oklahoma moves on to the season's final five weeks, getting back above .500 with the victory. Here are three takeaways after OU defeated Mississippi State. 1. Nothing is easy OU controlled the game, yet still won by only one score. In fact, if Taylor had been out there the whole time, it's not hard to envision the Sooners getting beat this week. Three missed field goals from Sandell took a lot of points off the board, and tight end Rocky Beers fumbled the ball after a long catch on a hurdle attempt. He also dropped a touchdown pass in the end zone. That's more points off the scoreboard for a team that doesn't score much. Penalties also hurt the Sooners: a chop block wiped out a third-down conversion and forced a missed field goal. An illegal formation penalty took a field goal off the board when Sandell missed the re-kick. Even if he had made it, the Sooners were lined up incorrectly again. Even against a backup quarterback, those mistakes turn what should've been an easy win into an eight-point victory. That's where OU stands as a program right now; even when they win, they make it look hard. 2. John Mateer did his job Quarterback John Mateer has drawn a lot of criticism for how he's played this season, and he's earned some of it. However, it's hard to have any problem with the way he played on Saturday. Mateer finished 22-for-29, with 283 yards and two touchdowns through the air. He also added nine carries for 37 yards. Most importantly, Mateer didn't turn the ball over. When he doesn't give it away, the Sooners have a chance. In fact, he was at his best against the Bulldogs , throwing his first touchdown on a scramble to his left, where he found an open Isaiah Sategna III and made the throw. His other TD came when he audibled into a shot play and threw to Beers over the middle. Mateer's stat line would have read three touchdowns, had Beers not let the ball get knocked out of his hands in the end zone. A play the SEC probably should have reviewed. item.content:encoded: The Oklahoma Sooners defeated the Mississippi State Bulldogs in Starkville on Saturday, winning 23-15 despite a sloppy performance. OU is now 4-3 overall and 2-2 in SEC play, and Brent Venables got the win over former assistant Jeff Lebby. OU was aided by MSU star quarterback Kamario Taylor missing the game's final three quarters, but the defense played well against both Taylor and backup Parker Puckett. Short of a double pass trick play touchdown and a late desperation TD and two-point conversion, the Sooners again put a lot of good on film on the defensive side of the ball. As expected, most of the mistakes came on the offensive side of the ball, but the OU special teams also had a poor day, especially kicker Tate Sandell. Oklahoma got a road win in the SEC, and those are hard to come by, but it's a game that the Sooners should have won by much more. Oklahoma moves on to the season's final five weeks, getting back above .500 with the victory. Here are three takeaways after OU defeated Mississippi State. 1. Nothing is easy OU controlled the game, yet still won by only one score. In fact, if Taylor had been out there the whole time, it's not hard to envision the Sooners getting beat this week. Three missed field goals from Sandell took a lot of points off the board, and tight end Rocky Beers fumbled the ball after a long catch on a hurdle attempt. He also dropped a touchdown pass in the end zone. That's more points off the scoreboard for a team that doesn't score much. Penalties also hurt the Sooners: a chop block wiped out a third-down conversion and forced a missed field goal. An illegal formation penalty took a field goal off the board when Sandell missed the re-kick. Even if he had made it, the Sooners were lined up incorrectly again. Even against a backup quarterback, those mistakes turn what should've been an easy win into an eight-point victory. That's where OU stands as a program right now; even when they win, they make it look hard. 2. John Mateer did his job Quarterback John Mateer has drawn a lot of criticism for how he's played this season, and he's earned some of it. However, it's hard to have any problem with the way he played on Saturday. Mateer finished 22-for-29, with 283 yards and two touchdowns through the air. He also added nine carries for 37 yards. Most importantly, Mateer didn't turn the ball over. When he doesn't give it away, the Sooners have a chance. In fact, he was at his best against the Bulldogs , throwing his first touchdown on a scramble to his left, where he found an open Isaiah Sategna III and made the throw. His other TD came when he audibled into a shot play and threw to Beers over the middle. Mateer's stat line would have read three touchdowns, had Beers not let the ball get knocked out of his hands in the end zone. A play the SEC probably should have reviewed. Oklahoma also trusted Mateer on key late plays to snuff out the MSU rally, and he made good decisions all day. It hasn't been the season he expected, but Mateer had it going this week. 3. On to the next Honestly, it's hard to learn anything new from this win. Mississippi State has the worst defense the Sooners have seen this year outside of UTEP, and OU's offense played its best since the season opener, despite making way too many mistakes. The Sandell misses are certainly concerning, but it's hard to see Oklahoma trying another kicker right now. The defense played as it typically does, as expected against a backup QB. Offensive coordinator Ben Arbuckle's early commitment to the run game was a good sign, but he has yet to show he can lean on the run in crunch time. OU will have plenty more opportunities to see if he's learned his lesson over the next few weeks. This team is what it is, but that was good enough in Week 8. A fourth win sets you up to finish your season strong, as the goal now is to set yourself up for the best bowl game possible at the end of the year and build momentum for next year. South Carolina comes to town on Halloween night, and Oklahoma will again need to find an offensive identity, bounce back on special teams, and rely on that defense to try and get consecutive wins for the first time all year. item.title: Clippers have glaring issue to fix before Thunder game, 'We didn’t play smart'
item.description: Darius Garland and the Los Angeles Clippers struggled to keep control of the ball throughout their crosstown rivalry game against the Los Angeles Lakers on Friday, Oct. 23. The Lakers (2-0) capitalized on those mistakes by the Clippers (1-1) and earned a 125-117 victory at Crypto.com Arena. The Clippers gave up 26 turnovers, including nine by Garland. It was a drastic increase from the 17 turnovers the team had in the 121-96 season-opening victory over the Sacramento Kings on Oct. 21. The Clippers finished the first quarter against the Lakers with a 31-27 lead but had eight turnovers take place during that period. The Clippers had only allowed nine total turnovers in the first half against the Kings. Clippers crumbled vs Lakers Lue’s team crumbled in the third quarter against the Lakers, giving up 10 turnovers and were outscored 39-26. “We had to be better,” Lue said. “They did a couple things, but we got to take care of the basketball. “You can’t play against a good team and turn it over 26 times and expect to win the game. We fought, we played hard, but we didn’t play smart.” The Lakers scored 33 points off those turnovers. The Clippers will take on the Oklahoma City Thunder , the toughest test for the team so far this season, on Sunday, Oct. 25. Through the first two games of the season, the Thunder have proven to have players that could generate turnover opportunities. The Thunder forced 13 turnovers, including three steals by Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, during their NBA Finals rematch against the San Antonio Spurs to open the season. The Thunder improved to 2-0 on the season after Ajay Mitchell and Cason Wallace combined for nine steals against the Denver Nuggets, who turned the ball over 22 times. This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Clippers have glaring issue to fix before Thunder game, 'We didn’t play smart'

item.title: BYU Cougars suffer heartbreaking upset defeat in double-overtime to UCF
item.description: Credit: Rob Gray-Imagn Images BYU Cougars suffer heartbreaking upset defeat in double-overtime to UCF appeared first on ClutchPoints . Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . Coach Kalani Sitake’s No. 2 BYU Cougars impressed Nick Saban with their win over Notre Dame , and then hit the road to take on the UCF Golden Knights at FBC Mortgage Stadium in Orlando, Florida. The Cougars were stunned by a score of 39-31, suffering their first loss of the season in double-overtime as the Golden Knights overcame tough-luck injury news . Fans were jubilant after news broke of the Golden Knights’ win as upset mania gripped college football for a second straight week. BYU came into this week ranked number one in the College Football Power Rankings after surging ahead of Notre Dame and the Miami Hurricanes following their huge upset win in Provo, Utah. They weren’t expecting Week 8 to be as difficult as the Notre Dame game going up against a 3-3 UCF team, but the Golden Knights proved to be more than up to the task of beating the visitors on the gridiron as they pulled out all the stops en route to a thrilling victory. The Cougars were outgained 463-373 on the day as the Golden Knights got 293 yards passing and three touchdowns from unlikely hero Keyone Jenkins at quarterback. Bear Bachmeier attempted to answer back but wasn’t able to get it done in the final period. He finished with 257 yards, two touchdowns and an interception. Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) A controversial roughing-the-kicker penalty allowed the Knights to score the game-winning touchdown, leading to frustrated Cougars fans afterward, who knew their team blew a great opportunity to put itself in position for a potential College Football Playoff berth. This was called a roughing the kicker penalty on BYU in double overtime that allowed UCF to score a touchdown instead. The Golden Knights took a 39-31 lead after given the automatic first down. pic.twitter.com/Fklqxe4lnj — Underdog CFB (@UnderdogCFB) October 24, 2026 Related: FAU star receiver achieves historic feat with 5-TD performance Related: UCLA’s undefeated streak hits mark not seen in over 20 years

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) A controversial roughing-the-kicker penalty allowed the Knights to score the game-winning touchdown, leading to frustrated Cougars fans afterward, who knew their team blew a great opportunity to put itself in position for a potential College Football Playoff berth. This was called a roughing the kicker penalty on BYU in double overtime that allowed UCF to score a touchdown instead. The Golden Knights took a 39-31 lead after given the automatic first down. pic.twitter.com/Fklqxe4lnj — Underdog CFB (@UnderdogCFB) October 24, 2026 Related: FAU star receiver achieves historic feat with 5-TD performance Related: UCLA’s undefeated streak hits mark not seen in over 20 years

item.title: Si Woo Kim is about to play one of the hardest rounds of his career
item.description: Si Woo Kim is about to face something he's never faced before Getty Images Si Woo Kim has known all kinds of pressure in his career. He won the Players Championship at 21. He’s played in majors and become a stalwart for the Internationals at the Presidents Cup. Kim also won the gold medal in the team competition at the 2023 Asian Games, earning an exemption from military service in South Korea. “I was still scared as [expletive],” Si Woo Kim told The Associated Press’ Doug Ferguson in March of his Asian Games win. But to try to win for other people, for home, that’s a pressure that can be crippling. “Last year, I thought I was OK, but it was super pressure,” Kim told the DP World Tour this week. I’ve never won in Korea. I want to win so bad. I had so much pressure last year. I think this year will be better, but it’s still going to be a lot of pressure from the home fans. So I’m excited to play, but also I really want to win too.” Kim has done his best so far this week to put himself in position to be the hometown hero — to achieve something close to his heart. He opened with rounds of 67, 69 and 67 to sit at 10 under through three rounds, just three shots off the pace set by Yuto Katsuragawa. At the 2019 Open Championship at Royal Portrush, Rory McIlroy shed tears as his valiant charge to make the cut in front of his home crowd came up short. “As much as I came here at the start of the week saying I wanted to do it for me, you know, by the end of the round there today I was doing it just as much for them as I was for me,” McIlroy said after his cut-line charge came up short at the 2019 Open Championship at Royal Portrush. “I wanted to be here for the weekend. item.title: Seahawks Part Ways With Hard Knocks Fan Favorite Before Chiefs Game
item.description: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - AUGUST 15: Montorie Foster Jr. #87 of the Seattle Seahawks reacts during the first quarter of the NFL preseason game against the Dallas Cowboys at Lumen Field on August 15, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Jack Compton/Getty Images) Getty The Seattle Seahawks have parted ways with one of the feel-good stories from their 2026 training camp. Seattle waived wide receiver Montorie Foster Jr. on Saturday, October 24, just one day before its Week 7 matchup against the Kansas City Chiefs. The move ends Foster’s stint on the active roster less than two months after he became a fan favorite during HBO’s “Hard Knocks.” The Seahawks announced the transaction Saturday, explaining that Foster was waived to make room for offensive guard Anthony Bradford, who was activated from injured reserve. Seattle also elevated linebacker Jimmy Ciarlo and defensive back Trevon Diggs from the practice squad ahead of Sunday’s game. Montorie Foster Jr.’s Seahawks Journey Takes Unexpected Turn Foster’s release marks a disappointing development for a player whose journey to the NFL captured the attention of Seahawks fans throughout the summer. After initially signing with Seattle as an undrafted free agent in 2025, Foster saw his first opportunity derailed by injury. He returned home, worked as a substitute teacher and earned his real estate license before getting another chance with the Seahawks. His comeback became a featured storyline on “Hard Knocks,” particularly as he battled to make the team’s initial 53-man roster. Foster backed up the television attention with a productive preseason, catching seven passes for 73 yards and a touchdown across three exhibition games. That performance helped him survive Seattle’s final roster cuts on August 30, a development Heavy covered at the time . The season finale of “Hard Knocks” featured Foster’s emotional phone call to his parents after learning he had made the team. His regular-season opportunities, however, were limited. Foster appeared in Seattle’s Week 1 victory over the New England Patriots , playing six special teams snaps. He had been a healthy scratch since Week 2, according to RotoWire. The 25-year-old will now be subject to the NFL’s waiver process. If he goes unclaimed, he can become a free agent and pursue another opportunity. Seahawks Activate Anthony Bradford Before Chiefs Game While Foster’s departure closes one chapter, the corresponding roster move gives Seattle an experienced offensive lineman back ahead of an important matchup. The Seahawks activated Anthony Bradford from injured reserve after the fourth-year guard missed five consecutive games. Bradford last played in Seattle’s Week 1 victory over New England before knee and hip injuries sidelined him. The Seahawks designated him to return to practice earlier this week, opening the door for Saturday’s activation. A fourth-round selection in the 2023 NFL Draft, Bradford has appeared in 43 career games with 39 starts. He started all 17

Foster backed up the television attention with a productive preseason, catching seven passes for 73 yards and a touchdown across three exhibition games. That performance helped him survive Seattle’s final roster cuts on August 30, a development Heavy covered at the time . The season finale of “Hard Knocks” featured Foster’s emotional phone call to his parents after learning he had made the team. His regular-season opportunities, however, were limited. Foster appeared in Seattle’s Week 1 victory over the New England Patriots , playing six special teams snaps. He had been a healthy scratch since Week 2, according to RotoWire. The 25-year-old will now be subject to the NFL’s waiver process. If he goes unclaimed, he can become a free agent and pursue another opportunity. Seahawks Activate Anthony Bradford Before Chiefs Game While Foster’s departure closes one chapter, the corresponding roster move gives Seattle an experienced offensive lineman back ahead of an important matchup. The Seahawks activated Anthony Bradford from injured reserve after the fourth-year guard missed five consecutive games. Bradford last played in Seattle’s Week 1 victory over New England before knee and hip injuries sidelined him. The Seahawks designated him to return to practice earlier this week, opening the door for Saturday’s activation. A fourth-round selection in the 2023 NFL Draft, Bradford has appeared in 43 career games with 39 starts. He started all 17 games during the 2025 season. His return gives Seattle another experienced option along an offensive line that has struggled to protect quarterback Sam Darnold. The Seahawks have allowed 16 sacks through their first six games, making Bradford’s availability particularly relevant ahead of a matchup with Kansas City. Seahawks Elevate Trevon Diggs, Jimmy Ciarlo for Chiefs Matchup Seattle’s Saturday roster activity extended beyond Foster and Bradford. The Seahawks also elevated defensive back Trevon Diggs and linebacker Jimmy Ciarlo from the practice squad for Sunday’s game. Diggs has appeared in three games for Seattle this season. His elevation comes just one day after the Seahawks released the former Pro Bowl cornerback from the active roster and signed him back to the practice squad. Ciarlo, meanwhile, made his Seahawks debut in the team’s Week 6 loss to the Denver Broncos . Both elevations provide additional defensive personnel options as Seattle prepares to face Patrick Mahomes and the undefeated Chiefs. The Seahawks enter Sunday’s matchup looking to snap a two-game losing streak. The latest moves bring additional experience back to the offensive line and reinforce the defensive depth chart, but they also come at the expense of one of the team’s most recognizable training camp success stories.
